load.optimalBody: Optimal: your recent load matches what you are used to.

info.monitorBody: Health Monitor compares last night’s vitals with your personal normal range: the average of your last 30 nights plus or minus one standard deviation. Blood oxygen also flags anything below 95%. A change in several vitals at once can be an early sign of illness. Pulse is not a medical device; if you feel unwell, talk to a doctor.
info.stressIntro: Stress Monitor scores how activated your body is, from 0 to 100, every 6 minutes: your heart rate against your awake heart rate over the last 30 days, and at night your HRV against its 30-day baseline.
info.stressLow: Low, 0 - 29: you might be feeling calm, relaxed or sleepy.
info.stressMedium: Medium, 30 - 59: neutral, alert or mildly activated.
info.stressHigh: High, 60 - 100: excited, stressed or highly activated.
info.stressNote: Workouts and exercise are left out, so a run never counts as stress. Stress is provisional until your data spans 30 days.
info.fitnessBody: VO2 max is the most oxygen your body can use during hard exercise. Pulse ranks it against people of your age and sex from the FRIEND registry. Training load divides your fatigue (about a week of workout load) by your fitness (about three weeks); above 1.4 is a spike.
info.healthspanBody: Pulse Age estimates how old your body behaves, from nine habits and vitals over the 28 days ending each Sunday. Pace of Aging is your Pulse Age divided by your age: 1.0x means your body behaves its age, below 1.0x younger, above 1.0x older. Both are estimates for personal insight, not a medical assessment.
info.hrBody1: Your band records heart rate through the day. The Google Health app shares it with Health Connect, and Pulse reads it from there.
info.hrBody2: While this screen is open on today, Pulse checks for new readings every minute. A reading usually arrives one to three minutes after your band takes it, so the newest one is never quite now.
info.hrBody3: The chart shows each minute’s average. Minutes without a reading, when the band was off or not syncing, stay blank.

hrv.info1: Your average overnight HRV over the last 7 nights, against your usual range, in the manner of Garmin’s HRV Status. Your usual range comes from the 60 nights before that, on a log scale, and needs 21 nights to form.
hrv.info2: Balanced: the 7-day average sits in your usual range. Unbalanced: above it, or a little below. Low: well below it, often a sign of strain, illness or poor sleep. A single night doesn’t move it much; a trend over days does.
hrv.info3: Garmin also shows Poor when your usual range is low for your age; Pulse leaves that out until it has a published age norm to compare with.
hrv.calibrating: HRV Status needs 21 nights of HRV to learn your usual range.
hrv.nights: Last 4 weeks of nightly HRV against your usual range of {{low}} to {{high}} milliseconds

heartRate.chartInfoBody: Heartbeats per minute across the selected day. Gaps mean no heart rate reading was available.
heartRate.zonesEmptyDay: No heart-rate zones on this day.

monitor.legend: Latest reading vs. the 30 days before it
monitor.illnessBody: Several vitals moved away from your normal range together, a pattern that often comes before feeling unwell. Consider an easier day and extra sleep.

stress.chartInfoBody: Body activation every 6 minutes, from 0 to 100. Workouts and exercise appear as excluded periods rather than stress scores.
stress.levelsInfoBody: Scored time outside workouts, split into low, medium and high activation. When available, the faded bar compares the same weekday in your recent history.
stress.trendInfoBody: Average activation across each day's scored time over the last 30 days. Days without enough data remain gaps.

hsText.sleepHours: Both short and long sleep are linked to higher mortality. Around 7.5 to 9 hours a night carries the lowest risk; 7 hours costs about half a year, 6 hours or less about 2.
hsText.sri: Being asleep at the same times each day is linked to a longer life, on top of how long you sleep. The reference is a consistency of 70: below it costs years quickly, above it takes a little off. The same Sleep consistency as on the Sleep screen, averaged over the window.
hsText.zone13: Moderate activity is linked to steeply lower mortality, with the reference at 150 minutes a week and the benefit levelling off well past it. Counted by Pulse from your heart rate in Zones 2 and 3 (60 to 80% of max heart rate), as a weekly average of the 28 days.
hsText.zone45: Vigorous activity adds benefit on top of moderate activity. The reference is 10 minutes a week; a little more helps, and the benefit levels off quickly. Counted from your heart rate in Zones 4 and 5.
hsText.strength: Muscle-strengthening work (strength training, weights, calisthenics or HIIT) is linked to lower mortality. The reference is 10 minutes a week, and the benefit levels off past about 40.
hsText.steps: More daily steps go with lower mortality. The reference is 8,000 a day (6,000 from 60), and credit stops at 10,000 (8,000 from 60). Days without heart rate or steps are left out, so a band left on the charger isn't read as a lazy day.
hsText.vo2max: Higher cardiorespiratory fitness is one of the strongest predictors of a longer life. The reference comes from a table for your age and sex; each ml/kg/min above it takes about 0.4 years off, each below adds about as much. From Fitbit's VO2 max readings.
hsText.restingHr: A higher resting heart rate is linked to higher mortality. The reference comes from a table for your age and sex; each 10 bpm above it adds about 1.2 years.
hsText.leanMass: The share of your weight that isn't fat. The reference is 100 less the typical body fat for your age and sex. Falling short of it costs years, faster the further you are; from 35, beating it takes a little off, more so with age. From your body fat readings.
hsText.bloodPressure: Sustained elevated systolic blood pressure is a major driver of cardiovascular risk. The reference is 115 mmHg systolic; protocol-grade upper-arm readings across multiple days contribute a bounded additive term to Pulse Age.

hs.vo2Estimate: Estimated from resting heart rate and activity
hs.leanNeeds: Needs body fat (a smart scale, or Journal › Log › Body fat), or your weight with your height in Profile. Left out of Pulse Age.
hs.leanCaptionEstimated: {{parts}}. Body fat estimated from your BMI.
hs.bpNeeds: Requires 12 protocol-grade readings across 3 days in the last 90 days ({{readings}}/12 readings, {{days}}/3 days). Left out of Pulse Age.
hs.bpCaption: Mean {{systolic}}/{{diastolic}} mmHg from {{readings}} readings across {{days}} days.

ecgText.normal: Your heart rhythm appears normal and shows no signs of AFib.
ecgText.afib: This reading shows signs of atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. Share it with your doctor.
ecgText.inconclusive: This reading couldn’t be classified, often because of movement, a weak signal or another rhythm.
ecgText.inconclusiveHigh: Your heart rate was over 120 bpm, too high to check your rhythm. Rest for a few minutes and try again.
ecgText.inconclusiveLow: Your heart rate was under 50 bpm, too low to check your rhythm.
ecgText.unreadable: The signal was too noisy to read. Try again sitting still with your arm resting on a table.
ecgText.notAnalyzed: This recording was saved but not classified, so it has no rhythm result.
ecgText.noResult: No rhythm result came with this recording.
